narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 68.9 percent chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. In other words, the model projected failure as more than twice as likely as passing, and that risk was too high for the school to accept.

The strongest factor was your third-year class position. You ranked in the second decile, while accepted applicants typically sat near the sixth. This low standing, coming so close to the end of your studies, strongly signaled that your academic performance would not translate into bar success. Your first-year ranking also hurt: you were in the third decile, again below the accepted average near the sixth, though this mattered less than your third-year performance.

Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor, but it worked in your favor. At 37, you were right at the accepted average of 37.18, so it pointed toward passing. However, this positive signal could not outweigh the combined negative impact of your two class rankings. The model saw strong bar-exam preparation as a bigger issue than standardized test ability.

To improve, you need to demonstrate a stronger academic record if you reapply. Focus on courses that mirror bar subjects and aim to substantially raise your class ranking, especially in your final year. A stronger LSAT could help, but your school performance is what most needs to change.
